cards.front: Parallel lines stay [ ___ ] and [ ___ ].
cards.back: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and never meet.

options.text: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and never meet.
options.explanation: Parallel lines remain a constant perpendicular distance apart, so they never converge or intersect, even when extended indefinitely in both directions.

options.text: Parallel lines stay different distances apart and never meet.
options.explanation: Lines whose separation changes are not parallel, even if they never meet in the part of the diagram shown. Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and never meet.

options.text: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and eventually meet.
options.explanation: Meeting lines cannot be parallel because parallel lines do not intersect, however far they are extended. Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and never meet.

options.text: Parallel lines stay closer and closer together and eventually meet.
options.explanation: Getting closer and eventually meeting describes converging lines, not parallel lines. Parallel lines maintain the same separation and never meet when extended.

cards.front: A transversal is a line that [ ___ ].
cards.back: A transversal is a line that crosses two or more other lines.

options.text: crosses two or more other lines
options.explanation: A transversal intersects at least two other lines at distinct points, creating the angle relationships used when those lines are parallel.
Crossing only one line does not create the two intersections needed for transversal angle relationships. A transversal crosses two or more other lines.

options.text: runs parallel to two other lines
options.explanation: Running parallel means the line does not intersect the other lines, whereas a transversal must cross two or more other lines.

options.text: meets two other lines at one point
options.explanation: Passing through a shared intersection is not the usual transversal arrangement because it does not create separate crossings. A transversal crosses two or more other lines.

cards.front: An angle next to 68° on a straight line is what?

options.explanation: Adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180°, so the missing angle is $180° - 68° = 112°$.
This repeats the given angle instead of using the straight-line total. Adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180°, giving $180° - 68° = 112°$.
This subtracts 68° from 190° rather than the straight-line total of 180°. The required angle is $180° - 68° = 112°$.
This uses the reflex-angle total of 360° instead of the 180° total for a straight line. The adjacent angle is $180° - 68° = 112°$.

cards.front: The angle vertically opposite 68° is what?

options.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the angle directly opposite the given 68° angle also measures 68°.
112° is the supplementary angle adjacent to 68°, found using a straight-line total. The vertically opposite angle is equal to 68°.
This incorrectly doubles the given angle. Vertically opposite angles are equal rather than added together, so the required angle is 68°.
This subtracts the angle from 90°, confusing vertically opposite angles with complementary angles. Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the answer is 68°.

cards.front: Angles in a triangle add to [ ___ ].
cards.back: Angles in a triangle add to 180°.

options.explanation: The three interior angles of every triangle have a total of 180°, regardless of the triangle’s side lengths or shape.
360° is the interior-angle total for a quadrilateral, not a triangle. The three interior angles of a triangle add to 180°.
90° is the size of one right angle, not the total for every triangle. A triangle’s three interior angles add to 180°.
270° can result from counting three right angles, but a triangle cannot contain three right angles. Its interior angles always total 180°.

cards.front: When parallel lines are cut by a transversal, what is true of corresponding angles?

options.explanation: For parallel lines, corresponding angles occupy the same relative position at the two intersections and therefore have equal measures.
Adding to 180° is the relationship for co-interior angles, not corresponding angles. When the lines are parallel, corresponding angles are equal.
Vertically opposite angles occur at the same intersection, whereas corresponding angles occur at different intersections. Corresponding angles are equal when the lines are parallel.
Corresponding angles may look separated in the diagram, but parallel lines ensure that angles in matching positions are equal, not unequal.

cards.front: Corresponding angles are in the [ ___ ] at each crossing.
cards.back: Corresponding angles are in the same relative position at each crossing.

options.explanation: Corresponding angles occupy matching locations around their two intersections, such as top-right at each crossing, so they are in the same relative position.
An opposite relative position identifies a different angle relationship rather than corresponding angles. Corresponding angles occupy the same relative position at each crossing.
Alternate positions are associated with alternate angles, which lie on opposite sides of the transversal. Corresponding angles occupy the same relative position at each crossing.
Vertically opposite angles are across from each other at one intersection, not at matching positions across two intersections. Corresponding angles use the same relative position.

cards.front: A top-right angle is 74°. The top-right corresponding angle is $x$. What is $x$?

options.explanation: Corresponding angles formed by a transversal crossing parallel lines are equal. Since both angles occupy the top-right position, $x = 74^\circ$.
This uses the supplementary-angle calculation $180^\circ - 74^\circ$, which applies to co-interior or adjacent angles. Corresponding angles are equal, so $x = 74^\circ$.
This doubles the given angle, but corresponding angles are not added together. Their matching positions make them equal, so $x = 74^\circ$.
This subtracts 74° from 90°, confusing the pair with complementary angles. Corresponding angles are equal, so $x = 74^\circ$.

cards.front: Alternate angles lie [ ___ ] and on [ ___ ].
cards.back: Alternate angles lie between the parallel lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.

options.text: Alternate angles lie between the parallel lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.
options.explanation: Alternate angles are the interior pair formed between the two parallel lines, with one angle lying on each side of the transversal.

options.text: Alternate angles lie between the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal.
options.explanation: Angles between the parallel lines on the same side of the transversal are co-interior angles. Alternate angles are between the lines on opposite sides of the transversal.

options.text: Alternate angles lie in corresponding positions and on the same side of the transversal.
options.explanation: Angles in matching positions on the same side are corresponding angles, not alternate angles. Alternate angles lie between the parallel lines on opposite sides of the transversal.

options.text: Alternate angles lie outside the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal.
options.explanation: This describes same-side exterior angles rather than alternate angles. Alternate angles lie between the parallel lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.

cards.front: When parallel lines are cut by a transversal, what is true of alternate angles?

options.explanation: For two parallel lines cut by a transversal, alternate angles form a matching pair on opposite sides of the transversal, so they have equal measures.
Supplementary angles add to 180°, which is the rule for co-interior angles. Alternate angles formed by a transversal across parallel lines are equal.
A 90° difference is not a parallel-line angle rule. When a transversal crosses parallel lines, each pair of alternate angles has equal measures.
Angles around a point add to 360°, but this does not describe a pair of alternate angles. Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal.

cards.front: One alternate angle is 49°. What is the other alternate angle?

options.explanation: Alternate angles formed when a transversal crosses parallel lines are equal. Therefore, an angle alternate to 49° must also measure 49°.
Subtracting 49° from 180° gives 131°, but that supplementary calculation applies to co-interior angles. Alternate angles are equal, so the other angle is 49°.
Subtracting from 90° incorrectly assumes the angles are complementary. Alternate angles across parallel lines are equal, so the other angle is 49°.
Doubling 49° does not follow any alternate-angle rule. Since alternate angles between parallel lines are equal, the required angle remains 49°.

cards.front: Co-interior angles are inside the parallel lines and on the [ ___ ] of the transversal.
cards.back: Co-interior angles are inside the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal.

options.explanation: Co-interior angles lie between the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal. Their measures consequently add to 180°.
Angles on opposite sides of the transversal are associated with the alternate-angle pattern. Co-interior angles instead lie on the same side of the transversal.
The definition does not depend on a fixed left-hand position, since a diagram can be rotated. Co-interior angles are on the same side of the transversal.
The right-hand position is not part of the definition and changes if the diagram is rotated. Co-interior angles lie on the same side of the transversal.

cards.front: What is true of co-interior angles on parallel lines?

options.explanation: Co-interior angles lie on the same side of a transversal between two parallel lines. They are supplementary, meaning their measures have a total of 180°.
Equality is the rule for alternate and corresponding angles, not generally for co-interior angles. Co-interior angles are supplementary and therefore add to 180°.
A total of 90° describes complementary angles, not co-interior angles. Co-interior angles on parallel lines are supplementary, so they add to 180°.
A total of 360° applies to angles around a point, not a co-interior pair. Co-interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°.

cards.front: If co-interior angles are 113° and $x$, what equation should you write?

options.explanation: Co-interior angles on parallel lines are supplementary, so their measures must total 180°. Adding the unknown angle to 113° gives the required equation.
Setting the angles equal confuses co-interior angles with alternate or corresponding angles. Co-interior angles add to 180°, so the equation is $x + 113^\circ = 180^\circ$.
Using 90° incorrectly treats the two angles as complementary. Co-interior angles are supplementary, so the correct equation is $x + 113^\circ = 180^\circ$.
Subtracting the two angle measures does not express their supplementary relationship. Their sum is 180°, giving the equation $x + 113^\circ = 180^\circ$.

cards.front: One co-interior angle is 118°. What is the other?

options.explanation: Co-interior angles on parallel lines add to 180°. Subtracting gives $180^\circ - 118^\circ = 62^\circ$, so the other angle is 62°.
Repeating 118° incorrectly applies the equality rule for alternate or corresponding angles. Co-interior angles add to 180°, so the other angle is 62°.
This results from using 190° as the supplementary total instead of 180°. The correct calculation is $180^\circ - 118^\circ = 62^\circ$.
This results from subtracting 112° rather than the given 118°, an easy digit-reading slip. Using 118° correctly gives $180^\circ - 118^\circ = 62^\circ$.

cards.front: An exterior 118° angle is on a straight line with a triangle’s inside angle. What is the inside angle?

options.explanation: The exterior angle and adjacent inside angle form a straight line, so they total 180°. Therefore, the inside angle is $180^\circ - 118^\circ = 62^\circ$.
Using the same measure confuses this pair with equal alternate angles. Adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180°, so the inside angle is 62°.
This comes from incorrectly using 190° as the angle total for a straight line. The correct total is 180°, giving $180^\circ - 118^\circ = 62^\circ$.
Halving the exterior angle does not find its adjacent angle. The two angles form a straight line, so subtraction from 180° gives 62°.

cards.front: A triangle has angles 38° and 62°. What is the third angle?

options.explanation: The interior angles of a triangle total 180°. Since 38° + 62° = 100°, the remaining angle is 180° - 100° = 80°.
This uses the sum of the two given angles as the missing angle. Triangle angles total 180°, so subtracting 100° gives the correct angle of 80°.
This incorrectly assumes the third angle is a right angle. The angle sum is 180°, and 180° - 38° - 62° gives 80°.
This comes from doubling the 38° angle rather than using the triangle angle sum. Subtracting both given angles from 180° gives 80°.

cards.front: What property of a parallelogram lets you use parallel-line angle facts on its sides?

options.explanation: A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides that are parallel. These parallel sides allow corresponding, alternate and co-interior angle facts to be applied.
Adjacent sides are not generally equal in a parallelogram; that is a property of a rhombus. Parallel-line angle facts apply because opposite sides are parallel.
Perpendicular diagonals are a property of some special parallelograms, such as rhombuses, but not all parallelograms. The relevant property is that opposite sides are parallel.
All angles are equal only in rectangular parallelograms, not in every parallelogram. Parallel-line angle rules can be used because opposite sides are parallel.

cards.front: Angle BAD is 124° and is co-interior with angle ABE. What is angle ABE?

options.explanation: Co-interior angles between parallel lines sum to 180°. Therefore angle ABE is 180° - 124° = 56°.
This treats co-interior angles as equal, confusing them with corresponding or alternate angles. Co-interior angles sum to 180°, so angle ABE is 56°.
This results from subtracting 124° from 190° rather than 180°. Co-interior angles are supplementary, so the correct calculation gives 56°.
This results from subtracting 124° from 170°, using the wrong total. Co-interior angles sum to 180°, giving angle ABE as 56°.

cards.front: In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite [ ___ ] are [ ___ ].
cards.back: In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite equal sides are equal.

options.text: In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite equal sides are equal.
options.explanation: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. The angles opposite those equal sides are the two equal base angles.

options.text: In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite unequal sides are equal.
options.explanation: Unequal sides have unequal opposite angles, not equal ones. In an isosceles triangle, it is the angles opposite the equal sides that are equal.

options.text: In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite equal sides are supplementary.
options.explanation: The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal rather than supplementary. They are the angles opposite the triangle’s equal sides.

options.text: In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite unequal sides are supplementary.
options.explanation: This combines two incorrect claims: unequal sides do not have equal opposite angles, and those angles are not necessarily supplementary. Angles opposite equal sides are equal.

cards.front: If EG = FG in triangle EFG, which base angles are equal?

options.explanation: Equal sides have equal opposite angles. Side EG is opposite the angle at F, while side FG is opposite the angle at E, so those angles are equal.
The angle at G lies between the two equal sides and is the vertex angle, not a base angle. The equal base angles are at E and F.
The angle at G is the vertex angle between EG and FG, so it is not one of the equal base angles. The equal angles are at E and F.
This incorrectly repeats the vertex angle rather than identifying the two base angles. Because EG = FG, the opposite angles at F and E are equal.

cards.front: Angle at F is 76° and $x$ is alternate to it. What is $x$?

options.explanation: Alternate angles formed when a transversal crosses parallel lines are equal. Since the angle at F is 76°, its alternate angle is also 76°.
This incorrectly treats the alternate angle as supplementary. Alternate angles are equal, so $x$ has the same value as the angle at F: $76^\circ$.
This halves the given angle, but alternate angles are copied directly rather than divided. Since they are equal, $x = 76^\circ$.
This assumes the alternate angle must be a right angle. Alternate angles are equal when the lines are parallel, so $x = 76^\circ$.
